title: Fragment 16 in Way's version
short: Arthur S. Way's 1920 rhymed version of fr. 16, a poem recovered from an Oxyrhynchus papyrus first published in 1914, with its damaged later lines filled out.
body: Fragment 16 was unknown until Grenfell and Hunt published papyrus P.Oxy. 1231 in 1914; it was still new when Arthur Sanders Way (1847-1930), translator of Homer and Euripides, included it in Sappho and the Vigil of Venus (1920). Way says in his preface that he wove together fragments in the same metre that might belong to one poem, and the archive's note warns that the joins are his. His heading describes Anactoria as having abandoned a girl-friend once dear to Sappho, which is his interpretation, not the papyrus. He keeps the Sapphic stanza and adds rhyme.

title: Priamel: horsemen, foot, ships
greek: οἰ μὲν ἰππήων στρότον οἰ δὲ πέσδων οἰ δὲ νάων
short: The poem opens with a priamel, a list of other people's choices that sets up the speaker's own: cavalry, infantry and fleets against 'what one loves'.
body: The Greek begins: some say an army of horsemen, some of foot-soldiers, some of ships is the most beautiful thing on the black earth, but I say it is whatever one loves. This rhetorical pattern (the 'priamel') is common in Greek lyric. Sappho's version is pointed because the rejected options are military, the values of epic; she sets eros up as the measure of beauty instead. Way keeps the three-part list ('horsemen or foot or galleys', galleys being oared warships) but turns 'whatever one loves' into 'my love', narrowing the general claim.

title: I say that my love of all is sweetest
greek: ἔγω δὲ κῆν' ὄττω τις ἔραται
short: Way personalises the Greek's general statement, that the most beautiful thing is 'whatever anyone loves', into a claim about 'my love'.
body: In the papyrus Sappho says the finest thing is 'that which a person desires' (ken' otto tis eratai). That is a claim about value, often read as an early statement that beauty depends on the lover. Way's 'my love of all is / Sweetest and rarest' turns the maxim into a declaration about one beloved. The change suits his reading of the poem as a personal reproach, but it weakens the general thesis that the Helen example is about to 'prove'.

title: Hear the proof
short: Sappho says it is 'altogether easy to make this understood by everyone', then gives a mythical example (Helen); Way's 'proof' keeps the argumentative tone.
body: Using a myth as evidence (a paradeigma) is a standard move in archaic poetry, from Phoenix's speech in Iliad 9 onwards. Sappho presents her lyric claim as something that can be demonstrated, giving the poem the outline of an argument: thesis, proof, application to the present (Anactoria). Way's 'I wot' ('I know') and 'fain' ('gladly') are deliberate archaisms, part of the high Victorian diction he also used for Homer.

title: Helen
short: Helen of Sparta, most beautiful of women, who left her husband Menelaus for Paris of Troy: Sappho makes her the proof that beauty is what one loves.
body: The example is surprising. In epic Helen is the object of everyone's desire, but Sappho makes her the one who chooses: the woman who far surpassed all mortals in beauty herself judged the finest thing to be the man she loved, and left everything for him. Critics have noted that Sappho neither blames nor excuses Helen here, unlike much Greek tradition; her contemporary Alcaeus condemns Helen as the ruin of Troy (frr. 42 and 283). Compare also the old men on the walls of Troy, who find Helen's beauty a sufficient reason for the war (Iliad 3.156-160). Way's lines fit the general sense, but see the next notes on what he adds.

title: Him who brought the glory of Troy to ruin
short: Way follows an early conjectural restoration of damaged lines, naming Paris as Troy's destroyer; the papyrus as now read says Helen left 'the best of husbands' and sailed to Troy.
body: The Greek of lines 8-9 is broken, and editors after 1914 filled the gaps in different ways. Way's line reflects a restoration in which Helen chooses the man who destroyed all Troy's glory, that is, Paris. Modern editions (Lobel-Page, Voigt, Campbell) print a text in which Helen 'left her husband, the best of men, and went sailing to Troy'. The difference matters: in the modern reading Helen's choice is defined by what she left behind, which suits the poem's theme of absence and longing, whereas Way inserts a moral consequence (Troy's ruin) that the surviving Greek does not state.

title: parent and child
greek: κωὐδὲ παῖδος οὐδὲ φίλων τοκήων πάμπαν ἐμνάσθη
short: Helen 'gave no thought at all to her child or her dear parents': the child is Hermione, the parents Tyndareus and Leda.
body: This detail is secure in the papyrus. Helen's daughter Hermione appears in the Odyssey (4.12-14) being given in marriage to the son of Akhilleus. Sappho's point is the overwhelming force of eros, which overrides every other tie. Way's 'Reckless all of parent and child, she lavished / On the alien love for her own undoing' adds a judgement ('for her own undoing') and a note of foreignness ('alien') that the Greek does not supply.

title: Troyward was ravished
short: 'Ravished' (carried off) makes Helen passive; the Greek has her actively go to Troy, though a damaged line may say that someone (perhaps Aphrodite) led her astray.
body: Ravish here keeps its older sense, 'to carry off by force' (OED), and Way's word brings the poem closer to the tradition of Helen's abduction. The surviving Greek uses active verbs for Helen's departure. A following line is fragmentary ('led her astray'), and editors supply different subjects, often Kypris (Aphrodite). Scholars therefore still debate how far Sappho shows Helen choosing freely and how far driven by a god, a question as old as Gorgias' Encomium of Helen.

title: Anactoria
short: A woman named only in this poem; in the Greek she is absent and longed for, but Way makes her the faithless one who has forsaken a friend.
body: In the papyrus the Helen example 'has reminded me now of Anactoria, who is not here', and Sappho says she would rather see Anactoria's walk and the bright sparkle of her face than Lydian chariots. Nothing in the Greek says that Anactoria has been unfaithful. Way, reading the fragment as a reproach, gives her a guilt the Greek lacks ('Such are you!', 'You have forsaken'), and his heading names the injured party as a girl-friend of Sappho's. Some scholars have suggested the name is a pseudonym or have identified her with an Anagora of Miletus named in ancient testimony; both ideas are speculative.

title: contemns
short: Contemn: to despise or treat with scorn (OED); Anactoria is one who scorns the happiness close at hand.
body: Way's line voices a familiar moral idea, that people undervalue what they have and want what is far away, which suits his reading of Anactoria as a forsaker. In Sappho's poem the logic runs the other way: it is the absent Anactoria whom the speaker longs for, so the emotion lies in absence rather than reproach. The verb is formal literary English, typical of Way's high style.

title: a reed wind-shaken
short: Way's image of fickleness comes from the Gospels ('A reed shaken with the wind?', Matthew 11:7), not from Sappho.
body: Jesus asks the crowds what they went into the wilderness to see: 'A reed shaken with the wind?' (Matthew 11:7; Luke 7:24), meaning someone weak and changeable, which John the Baptist was not. Way borrows the biblical phrase for Anactoria's inconstancy. The papyrus here is damaged (a few letters may suggest something bent or light), and Way's simile is best taken as one of the joins he admits to in his preface. Students should not quote it as Sappho's image.

title: footfall ... face in its beauty beaming
greek: ἔρατόν τε βᾶμα κἀμάρυχμα λάμπρον ἴδην προσώπω
short: From the Greek 'her lovely step and the bright sparkle of her face', which Sappho prefers to armies; Way transfers them from Anactoria to the forsaken friend.
body: This is the emotional centre of the poem: Sappho would rather see Anactoria's way of walking and the radiance of her face than Lydian chariots and armed infantry. The words amarugma ('flashing, sparkle') and lampron ('bright') give the face a brilliance that outshines the gleam of armour. Way turns the step into 'music' (an added image) and, more importantly, attaches it to the forsaken friend rather than to Anactoria, so the speaker's longing is redirected. In the Greek the woman whose step and face are desired is Anactoria herself.

title: horsemen and footmen ... panoply
greek: τὰ Λύδων ἄρματα κἀν ὄπλοισι πεσδομάχεντας
short: The Greek specifies 'the chariots of the Lydians and foot-soldiers fighting in armour'; Way omits the Lydians.
body: Lydia, the rich kingdom of western Asia Minor with its capital at Sardis, was the great power on Lesbos's horizon in Sappho's time; Lydian luxury and display appear elsewhere in her poems (fr. 96 compares a woman now living in Lydia to the moon). The ring-composition is clear: the poem returns at its close to the armies of its opening, now decisively outweighed. Way's 'panoply' (a full suit of armour, from Greek panoplia) keeps the military glitter but loses the concrete place-name.

anchor: What is best is set above
title: Sapphic stanza and the uncertain ending
greek: ἀλλ' ἄδυνατον γένεσθαι ... πεδέχην δ' ἄρασθαι
short: Way's last stanza draws on broken lines after the Lydian stanza, which seem to say that something cannot happen for mortals and to speak of praying to share.
body: Scholars disagree whether the poem ended with the Lydian stanza (a neat ring) or went on; the papyrus has traces of further lines that seem to speak of what is impossible for human beings and of 'praying to share'. Way builds these traces into a consoling close, in which remembering past happiness with prayer is better than forgetting, and he personifies Fortune. This ending is his reconstruction. Throughout he keeps Sappho's stanza shape, three long lines and a short final line ('Sweetest and rarest', 'Chose for her lover'), and adds a rhyme scheme Sappho did not use.
